source.name: NASA Global Mean Sea Level Trend from Integrated Multi-Mission Ocean Altimeters, Version 5.2
source.method: Global mean sea level from satellite altimetry (TOPEX/Poseidon, the Jason series, Sentinel-6), about every 10 days and averaged by us into calendar months; it includes the seasonal cycle and is corrected for the slow sinking of the ocean floor since the last ice age (glacial isostatic adjustment, which adds about 0.24 mm a year), so it shows the water's own rise.

world.text: Over the same months, 1993 to 2025, global average sea level measured by satellites rose 3.3 mm a year. Here: 2.7 mm a year.

scenarios.name: low emissions
plain: By 2050, experts project the sea here about 35 cm higher than its 1995 to 2014 average, on the low emissions path.
Experts give about a 2 in 3 chance it lands between 25 and 46 cm higher on that path. Faster ice-sheet loss could push this higher, outside this range.
So each high tide would come in about that much higher than in 1995 to 2014, and the sea would still be rising about 7.5 mm a year.

scenarios.name: low emissions
plain: By 2050, experts project the sea here about 35 cm higher than its 1995 to 2014 average, on the low emissions path.
Experts have low confidence in this path: it adds ice-sheet loss that is hard to predict, so they give no odds for it. Its middle range is between 25 and 49 cm higher.
So each high tide would come in about that much higher than in 1995 to 2014, and the sea would still be rising about 7.6 mm a year.
